title: UI & UX Design for Augmented Reality — Visual Exam Revision
description: UX design for augmented reality, animated: what AR is, its advantages, the five UX design elements (environment, movement, onboarding, interaction, user interface) and the ten AR UX design guidelines.

scenes.title: What is AR?
lines: Point your phone at your living room, and a sofa that doesn't exist appears next to your real plant.
That is augmented reality. An experience that mixes the real and the virtual.
Designers use real-world elements and context to create an immersive experience.
AR elements can be sound, video, animation, or an extension of real-world objects.

scenes.title: Advantages of AR
lines: Why do designers love AR? Four advantages.
One. It benefits from the user's context. The real world is already there, so unlike virtual reality, you don't build an environment from scratch.
Two. Reduced cognitive load. The information sits right where you need it.
Three. Multiple sources of information, so you can use multimodality: sight, sound, touch.
And four. Higher user engagement.

scenes.title: 5 UX design elements + mnemonic
lines: There are five UX design elements for AR.
Environment. Movement. Onboarding. Interaction. And user interface.
Remember them as: Every Moving Object Is UI. Because in AR, it really is.

scenes.title: Element 1: Environment
lines: Element one. The environment, which is seen from two perspectives.
First, the virtual elements embedded in the real world. The designer controls these.
Second, the user's real environment. The designer does not control it, and it changes from context to context.
As users move between places, the UI must adapt. And think about public versus private spaces, because comfort decides satisfaction.

scenes.title: Element 2: Movement
lines: Element two. Movement.
AR users are often on the move: walking, riding a bus, even running to finish a game task.
The boundary between real and virtual is blurred, so designers must allow for simultaneous interaction with both.
Factor in the user's real movement, and the transitions between real and virtual.

scenes.title: Element 3: Onboarding
lines: Element three. Onboarding.
Treat users as learners, and guide them through the experience.
It is crucial for first-time users, and even more important in AR, because interacting in a mixed environment is unfamiliar.
For example: move your phone slowly to scan the floor. Then tap to place the sofa.

scenes.title: Element 4: Interaction
lines: Element four. Interaction.
Interaction reveals a product's affordances and features. In AR, it is different, because real and virtual are blended.
Design at both the micro level, like one gesture, and the macro level, like the whole task flow.
And minimize physical input, so users are not overwhelmed. Holding a phone up for long is tiring.

scenes.title: Element 5: User interface
lines: Element five. The user interface.
It includes visual hierarchy, typography and aesthetics.
But in AR the interface is dynamic. The background is the real world, and it keeps changing.
So consider context, environment, and how virtual elements blend into the real scene. Design holistically.

scenes.title: 10 AR design guidelines + mnemonic
lines: Now the ten AR UX design guidelines.
Consider user contexts. Holistic experience. Safety. Devices. Clear space.
Hierarchy. Instructions and help. Direct interaction. Audio. And learn from existing designs.
Memory trick: Cats Hate Showers, Dogs Shake Hard In Dirty Alley Lakes.

scenes.title: Guidelines 1-2: Contexts and holistic experience
lines: Guideline one. Consider different user contexts. User needs change depending on where and how they use the app.
Create personas and use cases to cover these contexts, including interactions beyond the physical environment.
Guideline two. Focus on the holistic experience, not individual interactions.
Understand the whole user journey: before, during and after using the app, and fix every breakpoint along it.

scenes.title: Guidelines 3-4: Safety and devices
lines: Guideline three. Optimize the experience for user safety.
Playing an AR game while walking on a street can lead to accidents.
So design to reduce risk, and add safety features and warnings.
Guideline four. Optimize for devices. Not every device gives the same AR experience.
Be transparent. Tell users which devices are preferred, and which are compatible, to manage expectations.

scenes.title: Guidelines 5-6: Clear space and hierarchy
lines: Guideline five. Maintain visual clear space.
Placing virtual objects in the real world changes the space around the user. Give them breathing room. Minimalism helps.
Guideline six. Stick to visual hierarchy, even though the context keeps changing.
Consistent virtual elements and well-defined personas make hierarchy possible. The most important thing should stand out first.

scenes.title: Guidelines 7-8: Instructions and direct interaction
lines: Guideline seven. Provide clear instructions and help, covering onboarding, app requirements, and the modes of interaction.
Keep them concise and available when needed. In long sessions, don't nag, but keep help easy to reach.
Guideline eight. Focus on direct interaction where possible.
Let users rotate a three D object with touch and hand gestures. It is more immersive, more intuitive, and reduces physical strain.

scenes.title: Guidelines 9-10: Audio and learning from others
lines: Guideline nine. Make good use of audio.
Sound effects for characters and objects increase immersion. Audio cues give feedback, guide interaction, and create ambiance.
For accessibility, offer volume control and subtitles.
Guideline ten. Learn from existing AR designs. Study quality AR apps, then adapt, iterate, and add your own unique touch.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Recap. AR mixes real and virtual, uses the user's context, and reduces cognitive load.
Five elements: Every Moving Object Is UI.
Ten guidelines: Cats Hate Showers, Dogs Shake Hard In Dirty Alley Lakes.
Picture the sofa in your living room, and you will remember them all.
